title: TOXOPLASMOSIS & MICROSPORIDIOSIS: THE PROTOZOAN UVEITIS GUIDE

sections.title: CHAPTER 11: PRotoZoAN UVeItIS - Overview
sections.content: Toxoplasmosis: The protozoa Toxoplasma gondii is an obligate intracellular parasite which is estimated to infect up to 50% of the world’s population. Lifetime risk of ocular toxoplasmosis is around 18/100,000 in the UK, but up to 20 times this level in West Africa. (Source: Page 507-508)

sections.title: Geographic Pathogen Variation
content: Prevalence and incidence depend on socio-economic factors and circulating parasite genotypes.
Common locations: South America, Central America, Caribbean, tropical Africa.
Rare: China.
South America severity: More severe due to extremely virulent genotypes of the parasite.

branches: Definitive Host: The Cat (excretes oocysts in faeces)
Forms: Oocysts (faeces), Bradyzoite (encysted in tissue), Tachyzoite (actively proliferating)
Transmission: Cat faeces/contaminated soil, Raw/undercooked meat, Contaminated water, Transplacental

rows: Acquired infection now more important than congenital

content.explanation: Transmission rate increases from 15% (1st trimester) to 60% (3rd trimester); HOWEVER, disease severity is much greater if acquired in early pregnancy.

sections.title: Ophthalmic Clinical Features
content: Laterality: Affects both eyes in 40%.
Immunocompromise Sign: Suspect if both eyes are simultaneously active.
Symptoms: Asymptomatic finding, floaters, dVA (decreased Visual Acuity).
Vitritis: May have 'vitreous precipitates' (akin to KPs on posterior surface of PVD).
Retinitis: White, fluffy area when active; becomes circumscribed and pigmented as it heals.
Inactive State: Atrophic scar with pigmented border.
Satellite Lesions: Adjacent to old scars (commonly seen).
Retinal Vasculitis: Possibly four-quadrant periphlebitis.
'Headlamp in the fog': Indistinct pale lesion seen through 4+ vitreous haze.
Anterior Uveitis: Often with iIOP (increased Intraocular Pressure).

sections.title: Diverse Presentations & Complications
content: Scleritis
Punctate outer retinitis (quiet vitreous)
Punctate retinal lesions +/- vitreous activity
Large lesions (especially in the elderly)
Endophthalmitis-like presentation
Neuroretinitis
Serous retinal detachments
Pigmentary retinopathy
Complications: Cataract, Glaucoma, CNV (Choroidal Neovascularization) membrane

rows: Usually unilateral, large granuloma, no satellite scars.
Can mimic any uveitis; positive treponemal serology.
Pizza-pie appearance, minimal vitritis, HIV+ status.
Rapid progression, peripheral necrosis, prominent vasculitis.
Candle-wax drippings, systemic involvement, hilar adenopathy.
Hydrocephalus, cerebral calcification, hepatosplenomegaly, retinochoroiditis (bilateral, macula-affecting).
Usually asymptomatic; may have fever and lymphadenopathy.
Life-threatening: Encephalitis, intracerebral cysts, hepatitis, and myocarditis.

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigations
content: Primarily a clinical diagnosis.
Serology: Interpret positive results with caution (many adults are IgG positive).
IgM Antibodies: Suggest acquired infection.
Negative Serology: Should exclude the diagnosis.
PCR: Identification of T. gondii DNA in aqueous or vitreous samples may be helpful.

sections.title: Box 11.6: Indications for Treatment
content: Lesions involving disc, macula, or papillomacular bundle.
Lesions threatening a major vessel.
Marked vitritis.
Any lesion in an immunocompromised patient.

sections.title: Treatment Evidence & Protocols
sections.content: A Cochrane systematic review showed no level 1 evidence to support the efficacy of routine antibiotic or corticosteroid treatment for acute Toxoplasma retinochoroiditis in immunocompetent patients. There is level 2 evidence suggesting that long-term prophylactic treatment may reduce recurrences in chronic relapsing disease. In immunocompetent patients, the disease is self-limiting (unless sight-threatening). Recurrence is common; mean number of recurrences is two (wide range seen).

sections.title: Systemic Medical Management
content: Step 1: Initiation of ≥4 weeks of antibiotic therapy.
Step 2: Options include Co-trimoxazole OR Clindamycin/Sulfadiazine OR Pyrimethamine/Sulfadiazine/Folinic acid (requires weekly FBC) OR Atovaquone.
Step 3: Corticosteroids (Prednisolone) - MUST NOT be used without effective anti-toxo therapy. Use caution/avoid if immunosuppressed.
Special Cases: Spiramycin for maternal infection to reduce transplacental spread. Azithromycin used in some centers. Atovaquone active against bradyzoites and tachyzoites.

sections.title: Intravitreal & Pregnancy Management
content: Intravitreal Option: 1 mg clindamycin plus 400 μg dexamethasone (in immunocompetent patients).
Maternal Infection: Treat with spiramycin (named-patient basis).
Screening: Some countries perform serial antenatal serological screening to permit early treatment.

rows: Wash all fruit/vegetables; Avoid unpasteurized goat’s milk; Cook all meat thoroughly; Avoid handling cat litter (or use rubber gloves).
15–60% risk if acquired during pregnancy. No risk otherwise (even if recurrence of active disease during pregnancy).

sections.title: Microsporidiosis (Bonus Section)
content: Etiology: Protozoan obligate intracellular parasites (4 genera cause human disease).
Patient Profile: Usually seen in immunosuppressed (notably AIDS).
Systemic Disease: Chronic diarrhoea, respiratory infection.
Ocular Presentation: Keratoconjunctivitis with bilateral irritation, photophobia, and punctate keratopathy.
Associated Signs: Follicular conjunctivitis and/or anterior uveitis.
